prompt: What are the best practices for the C4 model?
completion:
Below is a “cheat‑sheet” of the most widely‑adopted, proven best practices for creating, maintaining, and using the C4 (Context‑Container‑Component‑Code) model in any software‑architecture setting. It’s organized by purpose (audience/level), diagram type, tooling, and long‑term upkeep. Feel free to cherry‑pick the items that match your team’s maturity and tool stack. --- ## 1. Core Principles (Simon Brown’s 5 “S”s) | # | Principle | Why it matters | How to enforce it | |---|-----------|----------------|-------------------| | 1 | **Simplicity** | Diagrams should answer the question *“What does this system do?”* without getting lost in low‑level detail. | Keep each diagram focused on its purpose; avoid “all‑you‑need‑to‑know” fluff. | | 2 | **Focus** | Different stakeholders need different views. | Use the correct level (Context, Container, Component, Code) for each audience. | | 3 | **Consistency** | Inconsistent naming or missing links break trust. | Create a style guide and enforce it via linting or diagram‑as‑code tools. | | 4 | **Clarity** | A diagram is communication, not a sketch. | Use clear labels, color‑coding, and simple arrows; avoid overlapping elements. | | 5 | **Progressive elaboration** | Start small, add depth only where needed. | Build from Context ➜ Container ➜ Component ➜ Code; each level refines the previous. | --- ## 2. Diagram‑Level Best Practices | Level | Audience | Focus | Key Do’s | Key Don’ts | |-------|----------|-------|----------|------------| | **Context** | Executives, partners, non‑tech stakeholders | “Who uses the system and how it fits in the ecosystem?” | • Show all external actors and systems.
• Highlight the main business value.
• Keep the diagram ≤ 10 elements. | • Don’t show internal internals.
• Don’t use technology‑specific icons. | | **Container** | Solution architects, ops, devs | “What runtime containers compose the system?” | • Show each major deployment unit (web app, API, database, queue, etc).
• Label technologies (Java, Node, SQL, Kubernetes).
• Add brief responsibilities. | • Don’t add classes or methods.
• Avoid naming “container” after an actual OS container if you mean a microservice. | | **Component** | Developers, maintainers | “How is a container structured internally?” | • Break down into logical modules.
• Use “uses” arrows only for *runtime* dependencies.
• Add a short description of each component’s responsibility. | • Don’t show every class; that’s the Code level.
• Avoid too many arrows – use grouping if possible. | | **Code** | Developers, architects | “What’s inside a component?” | • Show packages, classes, or key functions.
• Highlight public APIs.
• Keep the diagram to 1–2 screen width; split if needed. | • Don’t list every method.
• Avoid deep inheritance trees unless crucial. | **Tip:** Use *semantic grouping* (rectangles or colors) to show a “family” of components or “layer” (UI, business logic, persistence). --- ## 3. Naming & Labeling Conventions | Guideline | Example | |-----------|---------| | Keep names short, but meaningful. | `AuthService` instead of `AuthenticationAndAuthorizationServiceForUserManagement` | | Use domain terms, not technology terms. | `Order` instead of `OrderRepository` | | Prefix external integrations with `External::` or suffix `-API`. | `External::PaymentGatewayAPI` | | Add “Role” if it matters: `User` vs `Admin`. | `Admin::UserManagementAPI` | | For code level, use package or module names. | `com.company.project.payment` | --- ## 4. Diagrammatic Conventions | Symbol | Meaning | Notes | |--------|---------|-------| | Rounded rectangle | System/Actor | Use the same style for all actors. | | Rectangular box | Container | Add a technology tag inside. | | Rounded rectangle inside a container | Component | Label the box with the responsibility. | | Arrow with a thin line | “Uses” | Direction = “from” to “to”. | | Arrow with a dashed line | “Data flow” | Use only if you want to emphasize data movement. | | Label on arrow | “HTTP/REST” or “gRPC” | Keep arrow labels to one or two words. | | Color coding | Layer or criticality | Example: UI in blue, Business in green, Persistence in gray. | --- ## 5. Tooling & “Diagrams as Code” | Tool | What it does | Best for | |------|--------------|----------| | **Structurizr** | Cloud or self‑hosted; visual editor + DSL | Enterprise teams; want a web UI | | **C4-PlantUML** | PlantUML macros for C4 | Quick sketches; open‑source | | **Diagrams.net** + **C4 template** | Drag‑and‑drop | Teams with no codebase integration | | **Mermaid (with C4 plugin)** | Markdown‑friendly | Docs in MkDocs, Docusaurus | | **Graphviz + C4-PlantUML** | Automatic layout | Large diagrams that need to stay tidy | **“Diagrams as code”** advantages: 1. **Version control** – Commit to Git, diffable, reviewable. 2. **Automation** – CI pipeline can generate images and embed them in docs. 3. **Consistency** – Linting tools (e.g., `structurizr-lint`) catch missing tags. 4. **Re‑use** – Include modules across multiple diagrams with a single definition. --- ## 6. Keeping Diagrams Living | Action | Frequency | Tool | Why it matters | |--------|-----------|------|----------------| | Update when a new container/service is added | Every sprint | Structurizr or PlantUML repo | Prevents “architecture drift” | | Review with the team | Monthly | Meeting | Ensures everyone sees the same view | | Link diagrams to ADRs or decisions | As part of each diagram | Markdown links | Keeps rationale discoverable | | Tag diagrams with environment (`dev`, `prod`, `demo`) | Per diagram | Label in file name | Avoids mixing environments | | Export to static assets (PNG, SVG) for documentation | CI pipeline | `plantuml` or `structurizr` CLI | Provides ready‑to‑use images | **Tip:** Treat the C4 repo like a code repo: run `git commit`, `git push`, run CI to validate and publish diagrams. --- ## 7. Integration With Other Artifacts | Artifact | How it links to C4 | Tooling | |----------|-------------------|---------| | **Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)** | Reference ADR IDs on diagram elements | Markdown + `structurizr` link | | **Service Registry / API Catalog** | Show APIs on Component/Code level | OpenAPI, Swagger UI | | **Deployment Pipeline** | Link Container diagram to Helm/K8s manifests | CD pipeline step | | **Observability Dashboards** | Add “monitoring” component with alerting links | Grafana, Prometheus | | **Security Policies** | Add “Security” component and link to NIST/ISO docs | Policy-as-Code tools | --- ## 8. Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them | Pitfall | Symptom | Fix | |---------|---------|-----| | Too many elements in a Context diagram | Overcrowded, unreadable | Remove non‑critical actors; add sub‑diagrams | | Mixing “what” and “how” in the same level | Confused responsibilities | Keep “what” (responsibility) in the label, “how” (technology) in a tag or note | | Duplicate or contradictory names | Nomenclature confusion | Enforce a naming convention via linting | | Diagrams out of sync with code | Dead links, missing components | Automate diagram generation from the codebase (e.g., `plantuml` with `@startuml` blocks inside code comments) | | Ignoring non‑technical stakeholders | Poor adoption | Use Context diagrams to communicate business value; avoid jargon | --- ## 9. Sample “Starter Pack” (C4-PlantUML) ```plantuml @startuml ' ---- Context ---- !include https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/master/C4_Context.puml Person(customer, "Customer") System_Boundary(s1, "E‑Commerce") { System(webapp, "Web Application") System(api, "REST API") System_DB(db, "Database") } Rel(customer, webapp, "orders, browses") Rel(webapp, api, "REST API calls") Rel(api, db, "CRUD operations") ' ---- Container ---- !include https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/master/C4_Container.puml Container_Boundary(s2, "E‑Commerce Containers") { Container(webapp, "React Frontend", "JavaScript") Container(api, "Spring Boot API", "Java") Container(db, "PostgreSQL", "Database") } Rel(webapp, api, "HTTPS") Rel(api, db, "JDBC") ' ---- Component ---- !include https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/master/C4_Component.puml Container_Boundary(c1, "API Containers") { Component(orderSvc, "Order Service", "Handles order placement") Component(authSvc, "Auth Service", "Handles authentication") } Rel(api, orderSvc, "Calls") Rel(api, authSvc, "Auth") @enduml ``` > Save the file as `ecommerce.puml`, run `plantuml ecommerce.puml` → PNG/SVG diagrams. > Add to your repo; CI can auto‑generate and push to a documentation site. --- ## 10. Checklist for a Healthy C4 Practice 1. **Scope & Audience** – Identify who will see each diagram level. 2. **Style Guide** – Create a one‑page guide (names, colors, arrow types). 3. **Tooling Stack** – Pick a diagram‑as‑code tool that fits your repo workflow. 4. **Version Control** – Store all `.puml`, `.txt`, or DSL files in Git. 5. **Automated Validation** – Add lint or CI step to detect missing tags. 6. **Link to ADRs** – Include ADR IDs or links in the diagram. 7. **Keep it Updated** – Schedule diagram reviews on sprint or release cadence. 8. **Export for Docs** – Generate PNG/SVG for static sites or PDF. 9. **Monitor Drift** – Run static analysis on CI to flag outdated diagrams. 10. **Educate Stakeholders** – Run a quick workshop on reading & contributing to C4 diagrams. --- ### Final Thought The C4 model is *not* a silver bullet for all architecture needs. Treat it as the *communication backbone* that ties together code, decisions, and business context. By following the practices above, you’ll get diagrams that are **simple, focused, consistent, clear, and evolvable**—exactly what any healthy software organization needs.
